title: India Won't Export Sugar for Years. El Niño, Ethanol and a Weak Monsoon Are All Squeezing at Once.
excerpt: With inventories at their lowest in three decades, cane farmers switching crops, and ethanol devouring what's left, the world's second-largest sugar producer has no sweetness to spare — and the diaspora's mithai bill is about to go up.
body:
India slammed the door on sugar exports in May, banning all outbound shipments until at least September 2026. In normal years, that kind of move would draw a shrug. India's domestic sugar appetite is enormous — around 28.5 million tonnes a year — and the government has always put Indian consumers first.

But this isn't a normal year. The ban didn't arrive because India has too much sugar. It arrived because India may not have enough.

Three Crises Converging

Start with the sky. Japan's Meteorological Agency confirmed in June that El Niño conditions have formed across the equatorial Pacific, and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration now estimates a 67 per cent probability of a "super El Niño" — the strongest ever recorded. India's weather office has already downgraded its monsoon forecast to 90 per cent of the long-term average, the weakest in 11 years. By late June, actual rainfall was running 43 per cent below normal. Central India — the sugarcane belt spanning Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka — recorded a 64 per cent deficit.

For farmers, the math is simple. Sugarcane is one of the thirstiest crops on earth. Growing a single kilogram of sugar requires roughly 1,500 litres of water. When the rain doesn't come, they switch to something else. In Maharashtra's Sangli district, cane growers are planting soybeans instead. In Uttar Pradesh, demand for cane seedlings has "fallen sharply," according to nursery owners, and the once-dominant Co-0238 variety has lost its productivity edge without a viable replacement.

Then there's the ethanol problem. India has committed to blending 20 per cent ethanol into petrol by 2025-26, a target it has aggressively pursued to reduce its $130-billion-a-year crude oil import bill. But half of India's ethanol comes from sugarcane — and every tonne of cane diverted to ethanol is a tonne that doesn't become sugar. Industry estimates suggest ethanol demand could more than double to 30 billion litres by 2039-40. Right now, that ambition is eating into sugar stocks.

> "In Uttar Pradesh, demand for cane seedlings has "fallen sharply," according to nursery owners, and the once-dominant Co-0238 variety has lost its productivity edge without a viable replacement."

Inventories at 30-Year Lows

The numbers are stark. India was expected to produce 30.95 million tonnes of sugar in the current season. Output is now forecast at 27.9 million tonnes — below domestic consumption for a second consecutive year. Opening inventories for the next season starting October are likely to fall to about 3.5 million tonnes, the lowest in more than three decades.

![Uttar Pradesh — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1d/Taj_Mahal_%28Edited%29.jpeg)

Of the 1.59 million tonnes originally cleared for export, about 800,000 tonnes were contracted, and the government pulled the plug before the rest could move. India has gone from being the world's second-largest sugar exporter to a country with zero tonnes available for international buyers.

"The government's policy is very clear," Ashwini Srivastava, Joint Secretary for Sugar at the Department of Food and Public Distribution, told trade publication ChiniMandi this week. "The topmost priority is meeting domestic consumption, the second is ethanol production, and only thereafter comes exports."

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the 37 million Indians living overseas, the ripple effects are already arriving. Global sugar prices have climbed, with benchmark futures buoyed by India's absence from the export market and El Niño fears over Brazil and Thailand's production.

That matters at the counter of every Indian sweet shop from Jackson Heights to Southall to Dubai's Al Karama. Mithai, the backbone of diaspora celebrations — Diwali boxes, wedding platters, temple prasad — is heavily reliant on sugar, and many specialist shops source directly or indirectly from Indian supply chains. When India's sugar gets scarce, raw material costs for these businesses climb.

More broadly, food inflation driven by a weak monsoon will squeeze household budgets in India, increasing the pressure on diaspora remittances. India received a record $140 billion in remittances in the latest fiscal year, and a meaningful share goes toward supporting families already stretched by rising prices.

No Quick Fix in Sight

Unlike an oil shock, which can be moderated by tapping strategic reserves or diversifying suppliers, a sugar shortage tied to climate and crop cycles plays out slowly. Even if the monsoon recovers in July, cane planted late produces lower yields the following season. Reuters reported this week that India "likely won't export sugar for years" — not months.

The government insists domestic supplies are "comfortable" and prices "reasonable." Ex-mill rates in Muzaffarnagar are holding at ₹4,150–4,260 per quintal. But comfort is relative. With El Niño strengthening, ethanol targets climbing, and cane acreage shrinking, India's sugar economy is being squeezed from every direction at once.

For a country whose culture runs on sweetness — from chai to celebrations — the bitter forecast is hard to sugarcoat.
